# What Bash is {#sec-overview .unnumbered}

Bash is the shell of most Linux machines, clusters, and continuous integration
runners: a program that reads a line, turns it into the call of another
program, and shows what it prints. It is both the interface for working on a
machine and a language for scripts, which are the same lines saved in a file.
Its unit of work is the program, not the function: a script starts programs,
hands each the output of the one before, and decides by their exit status what
to do next.

In research software, Bash is the glue around the code that does the science.
It writes the job scripts for Slurm ([](../tools/scheduling/slurm.qmd)), the
steps of continuous integration
([](../tools/version-control/github-actions.qmd)), the `%post` section of an
Apptainer definition file and the `RUN` lines of a Dockerfile
([](../tools/containers/index.qmd)), and the commands of a Makefile; and it is
how one finds, copies, and inspects files on a cluster.
It is weak at everything else: it has strings, integers, and arrays, but no
floating-point numbers or real data structures, its quoting rules are a source
of defects, and its error handling is minimal. Beyond a screenful of logic, or
as soon as a script computes something, write it in [](python.qmd) or [](r.qmd)
and let Bash start it (@sec-glue).

Working in Bash comes down to a mental model (@sec-model), the common commands
and constructs (@sec-syntax), and a few tools (@sec-tooling). The rules at the
end (@sec-rules) apply the principles to Bash.

Bash is the default shell of most Linux distributions; macOS ships Bash 3.2 and
uses zsh by default, so a script for both avoids newer features, such as
associative arrays. Checked against Bash 5.2 and ShellCheck 0.11.

| [-@sec-strict] | [](#sec-strict) | Start every script with `set -euo pipefail`. |

| [-@sec-glue] | [](#sec-glue) | Keep Bash for starting programs, and put computation in library code. |

# How Bash thinks {#sec-model}

Four facts explain most of the surprises of Bash: the shell, not the program,
expands what you type (@sec-commands); programs are connected by streams of
text (@sec-streams); every value is a string that the shell splits into words
(@sec-words); and a failing command does not stop a script (@sec-failure).


## A line is expanded, then split into a program call {#sec-commands}

The shell reads a line, expands it, and starts the first word as a program with
the other words as its arguments. Expansion replaces `$name` by the value of a
variable, `$(cmd)` by the output of a command, `~` by the home directory, and a
pattern such as `*.csv` by the list of the matching files. The program never
sees the pattern: with `wc -l *.csv`, `wc` receives the names of the files.
Quotes group words and are removed before the program starts.


## Programs are connected by streams of text {#sec-streams}

A program reads from its standard input, writes to its standard output, and
reports problems on its standard error. The shell connects them: `|` passes the
output of one program to the input of the next, and `>` sends it to a file.
Small programs that each do one thing, such as `sort`, `uniq`, `cut`, and
`grep`, are then combined into a pipeline, without a program of their own:

```bash
cut -d, -f2 table.csv | tail -n +2 | sort -n | uniq -c   # count each value
```


## Every value is a string, split into words {#sec-words}

A variable holds a string, and an unquoted expansion is split at spaces and
tabs, and then matched against files, before the command sees it. A name with a
space becomes two arguments:

```bash
name="my file.csv"
wc -l $name       # wc -l my file.csv: two files, neither exists
wc -l "$name"     # wc -l 'my file.csv': one file
```

The fix is to quote every expansion (@sec-quote). Only the numbers are
different: Bash calculates with integers, in `$(( 7 % 3 ))`, and has no floats;
`$(( 1 / 2 ))` is `0`. For anything else, call `awk`, `bc`, or Python.


## A failing command does not stop the script {#sec-failure}

Every program ends with an exit status: 0 for success, anything else for
failure. By default, Bash runs the next line whatever the status, so a script
whose first step failed goes on, with the output of the step missing, and
can finish with a status of 0 and a wrong result. `$?` holds the status of the
last command, `&&` runs the next command only after success, and `||` only
after failure. The remedy is to make failure stop the script (@sec-strict).


# Commands and constructs {#sec-syntax}

The following is the part of Bash that most scripts are made of.


## Files and directories {#sec-files}

```bash
pwd                          # the current directory
ls -lh                       # list, with sizes; -a includes hidden files
cd results/                  # change directory; cd - goes back, cd goes home
mkdir -p results/2026/raw    # create a directory with its parents
cp -r data/ backup/          # copy; -r for directories
mv old.csv new.csv           # move or rename
rm old.csv                   # delete for good; there is no trash. -r: directory
ln -s /data/raw raw          # a symbolic link
touch flag.txt               # create an empty file, or update its time
chmod +x run.sh              # make a script executable
find . -name "*.csv" -mtime -7    # the CSV files changed in the last 7 days
du -sh data/*                # the size of each item
df -h /scratch               # free space of a file system
```


## Look at and transform text {#sec-text}

```bash
cat file.txt                 # print a file; less file.txt to page through it
head -n 5 file.csv           # the first 5 lines; tail -n 5 the last 5
tail -f job.log              # follow a file as it grows
wc -l file.csv               # the number of lines
grep -n "error" job.log      # lines with a match, numbered; -i ignores case
grep -rl "alpha" src/        # the files under src/ that contain a text
sort -n -k2 -t, file.csv     # sort numerically by the 2nd comma-separated field
uniq -c                      # count adjacent equal lines; sort first
cut -d, -f1,3 file.csv       # columns 1 and 3 of a CSV file
tr 'a-z' 'A-Z'               # translate characters, from standard input
sed 's/old/new/g' file.txt   # replace text; -i edits the file in place
awk -F, '{ s += $2 } END { print s / NR }' file.csv   # mean of column 2
column -s, -t file.csv       # show a CSV file as a table
```

`awk` is a small language for tables of text, and enough for sums and means over
a column. These tools cut a CSV file at every comma, so a field that contains a
comma in quotes breaks them; use a CSV parser, such as pandas, for such files.


## Redirection and pipes {#sec-redirect}

```bash
cmd > out.txt          # standard output into a file, overwriting it
cmd >> out.txt         # appended to it
cmd < in.txt           # a file as standard input
cmd 2> err.txt         # standard error into a file
cmd > all.txt 2>&1     # both streams into one file
cmd 2> /dev/null       # discard the errors
cmd1 | cmd2            # the output of cmd1 is the input of cmd2
cmd | tee out.txt      # to the screen and to a file
find . -name "*.csv" -print0 | xargs -0 wc -l   # run a command on a list
```


## Variables, quoting, and substitution {#sec-variables}

```bash
sample="alpha"                        # no spaces around =
echo "sample is $sample"              # double quotes expand variables
echo 'sample is $sample'              # single quotes do not
today=$(date +%F)                     # the output of a command: 2026-03-01
echo "${sample}_1.csv"                # braces end the name of the variable
echo "${threads:-4}"                  # 4 if threads is unset or empty
echo "${1:?usage: run.sh INPUT}"      # stop with a message if $1 is missing
f="data.tar.gz"
echo "${f%.gz}" "${f##*.}"            # data.tar and gz: cut a suffix, a prefix
files=(a.csv b.csv)                   # an array
echo "${#files[@]}" "${files[@]}"     # its length, and all its items
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=8              # visible to the programs that it starts
```


## Conditionals and loops {#sec-control}

```bash
if [[ -f "$input" && -s "$input" ]]; then    # exists and is not empty
    echo "found"
elif [[ -d "$input" ]]; then                 # a directory
    echo "directory"
else
    echo "missing" >&2                       # an error goes to standard error
fi

[[ "$mode" == "fast" ]]                      # strings; -eq, -lt for integers
[[ -z "$name" ]]                             # is empty; -n: is not

for f in data/*.csv; do                      # the files that match
    echo "$f: $(wc -l < "$f") lines"
done
for i in {1..3}; do echo "$i"; done          # 1 2 3
while read -r line; do                       # a file, line by line
    echo "$line"
done < list.txt

if grep -q "error" job.log; then echo "failed"; fi   # test a command directly
```

`[[ ... ]]` is the test of Bash; the older `[ ... ]` needs more quoting. `if`
tests the exit status of a command, and any command can be the test.


## Scripts, arguments, and functions {#sec-script}

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

usage() {
    echo "usage: $0 INPUT_DIR OUTPUT_FILE" >&2
    exit 2
}

[[ $# -eq 2 ]] || usage            # $# is the number of arguments
input_dir=$1                       # $1, $2 ... are the arguments; $@ all
output=$2

count_rows() {                     # a function: arguments are $1, $2 ...
    local file=$1                  # local: not visible outside the function
    echo $(( $(wc -l < "$file") - 1 ))
}

for f in "$input_dir"/*.csv; do
    echo "$f: $(count_rows "$f") rows"
done > "$output"
```

Run it with `bash run.sh data/ rows.txt`, or, after `chmod +x run.sh`, as
`./run.sh data/ rows.txt`. The first line says which program runs the file.


## Move and fetch data {#sec-transfer}

```bash
ssh user@cluster                           # a shell on another machine
rsync -avP data/ user@cluster:/scratch/data/   # copy, resumable
scp results.csv user@cluster:~/            # copy one file
curl -fLO https://example.org/data.csv     # download; -f fails on an HTTP error
tar -czf data.tar.gz data/                 # pack and compress a directory
tar -xzf data.tar.gz                       # unpack
sha256sum data.csv                         # a checksum, for records and checks
```


## Processes {#sec-processes}

```bash
cmd &                  # run in the background; wait waits for all of them
jobs                   # the background jobs of this shell
ps aux | grep python   # the running processes
kill 12345             # ask a process to stop; kill -9 forces it
nohup cmd > out.log 2>&1 &    # keep running after the terminal closes
```

On a cluster, long work goes through the scheduler
([](../tools/scheduling/slurm.qmd)), not through a background job on the login
node. For an interactive session that survives a lost connection, use `tmux`.


# Tooling {#sec-tooling}

| Job | Tool |
|-------------------------------|---------------------------------------------|
| Find defects in a script | ShellCheck |
| Format a script | shfmt |
| Tests | Bats, which runs a script's functions and commands and checks their output and status |
| Check the syntax without running | `bash -n script.sh` |
| Debug | `bash -x script.sh`, which prints every command after its expansion |

```bash
shellcheck run.sh          # lint; -x follows the files that it sources
shfmt -w run.sh            # format in place
```

ShellCheck finds the defects of this document: unquoted expansions, `ls` in a
`for` loop, an `rm -rf` of a variable that may be empty, and unused variables.
It checks only the script, so a test with a small input and a known output
([](../principles/testing.qmd#sec-known-answers)) remains necessary.


# Rules {#sec-rules}


## Start with strict mode {#sec-strict}

Every script should start, after its first line, with `set -euo pipefail`.
`-e` stops the script at the first command that fails, `-u` treats an unset
variable as an error, and `pipefail` makes a pipeline fail if any of its
programs fails, not just the last. Without it, a script goes on after a failed
download or a typing error in a variable name, and writes a plausible, wrong
result ([](../principles/design.qmd#sec-loud)); with it, the script fails where
the problem is.

`-e` does not apply to a command that is the test of an `if`, or a part of a
`&&` or `||` list other than the last, so it is not a substitute for checking
what matters. And it stops the script at a `grep` that finds nothing,
as at any command with a non-zero status; where that is expected, say so with
`|| true` or test it in an `if`.


## Quote every expansion {#sec-quote}

Every expansion should be in double quotes, `"$var"`, `"$(cmd)"`, and `"$@"`
for all arguments, unless the splitting into words is the intention, and then
name it, for example with an array. An unquoted expansion is split at spaces and
matched against files (@sec-words), so a path with a space becomes two
arguments, and an empty variable vanishes from the command:

```bash
rm -rf $dir/*      # with dir empty: rm -rf /*
rm -rf "${dir:?}"/*   # stops with an error if dir is unset or empty
```

Quoting is cheap and fixes a whole class of defects that depend on the data
and the machine, which is what makes them hard to find.


## Check scripts with ShellCheck {#sec-shellcheck}

Every script should pass ShellCheck without findings, or with findings that are
turned off on the line itself with a comment that says why
(`# shellcheck disable=SC2086 # splitting is intended`). Run it before every
commit, or in continuous integration
([](../tools/version-control/github-actions.qmd)). It finds the defects of the
two rules above and others that nobody sees by reading, such as `[ $a = b ]`
with an empty `$a`, and it costs a second, which ranks it among the cheapest
tests that a script can have.


## Bash starts programs, library code computes {#sec-glue}

A script should start programs, connect them, and check their exit status, and
should not do the science itself. Bash has no floating-point numbers, no
structures, and no way to test a function in isolation, so a calculation, a
parser, or a decision based on the data belongs in library code
([](../principles/design.qmd#sec-library)), which has tests
([](../principles/design.qmd#sec-testing)), and the script calls it. A script
with more than about a screenful of logic, or with a loop that contains an
`if` that contains a pipeline, has outgrown Bash; rewrite it in Python or R
([](../principles/design.qmd#sec-kiss)).
